title: 1381: The Uprising
subtitle: Peasants' Revolt
author: Ars Historica
description:
In the summer of 1381, England's poorest rose up and nearly brought a king to his knees.

For three decades, the crown had squeezed the peasantry with impossible taxes and laws that bound them to their lords. When collectors came for a fourth poll tax, the rage that had been simmering in the fields and villages exploded. From Essex and Kent, tens of thousands marched on London. They burned the Savoy Palace, stormed the Tower, and forced a boy-king to grant them charters of freedom. For six days, the realm hung in the balance.

This is the story of that uprising, told through the documentary record that survived it — the chronicles, court rolls, and indictments that captured what the rebels wanted, who led them, and what happened when the crown turned to settle accounts. It is a history of manorial bondage and plague-driven labor shortage, of poll-tax revolts and a radical priest's vision of a leveled world, of Wat Tyler and John Ball and the nameless thousands whose names we will never recover. It traces how a medieval kingdom responded to the largest popular insurrection of its age, and what the Rising changed — and what it did not.

The historical record holds genuine gaps and competing readings. This account follows the evidence where it leads, and leaves the questions open.

Approximately 90 pages and 1 hr 53 min to read.

title: It Came From Iowa
subtitle: A GLMZ Novella
author: MindAttic
description:
Before dawn, Wes walks out to the north field following a sound he has never heard — low, sustained, between a chord and a groan. He finds an unregistered Behemoth, collapsed and inert, one tine snapped at the joint. And the machine he has grown up alongside is nudging the dead hull with a manipulator arm, pausing, nudging again.

Waiting for a response that is not coming.

At dawn, the machine begins moving south. Straight line. Five miles per hour. No transponder. No kill-switch response. Wes cuts cross-field to the grain elevator, climbs to the platform, and jumps across as the Crown passes level. His terrier, Pip — small, fearless, entirely certain this is his business — trots alongside at the base of the tines.

Fifty miles away in Dixon, Illinois, CJ Anderson's alert board lights up at 0614. Her commander wants demolition assets pre-authorized. She asks for time. He gives her less than she wants.

The Eigenlift interdiction drones go up in formation. The scythe-arm brings them down clean — no urgency, no strategy, the same motion as waving away a fly. By the third wave the footage looks like the Empire State Building and everyone watching knows it.

The machine just walks. Nobody can make it stop. Nobody yet knows why it started.

Wes does. He was there in the north field.

IT CAME FROM IOWA is a story about a machine that outlived its context — and the two people trying to understand it before the sky decides.

title: Irish Outlaws
subtitle: Three Centuries of Asymmetric Warfare
author: Ars Historica
description: In 1601 an Irish army lost a battle at Kinsale and never came back. For the next three hundred and twenty years, anyone in Ireland who wanted to decide what happened on their own ground had to do it as a criminal. RESISTANCE follows eight of them. Hugh O'Neill, who nearly took Ireland off Elizabeth I and lost it in a single afternoon. Patrick Sarsfield, who rode five hundred horse around an army in the dark and blew up its guns. Edmund O'Dwyer in the Glen of Aherlow with a price on his head. Michael Dwyer, who held the Wicklow Mountains for five and a half years until the British built a road to reach him. Anne Devlin, half-hanged in a Dublin garden and silent through years in Kilmainham after, who died destitute in a rented room half a century later. Robert Emmet, whose rising lasted an evening and whose speech has lasted two centuries. Michael Davitt, one-armed, who invented the boycott. Michael Kilroy, who took a machine gun off the Black and Tans at Carrowkennedy and died in his own bed in 1962 with the President of Ireland at his funeral Mass. Almost none of them knew about the others — Anne Devlin was Michael Dwyer's cousin, and that is the only thread between any two of them. All of them arrived at the same answer regardless. This is a book about what happens after the last real army is gone: the ambush, the informer, the burned townland, the price on the head, the ballad that outlives the man. It is grounded in the documentary record throughout — bounty warrants, witness statements, memoirs, court rolls — and it does not flinch from what that record shows about either side. Nobody in these pages gets out with clean hands. They went anyway. That is the whole story, and it is worth three hundred years of telling.

title: Jeanne d'Arc
subtitle: Prophecy or Pathology?
author: Ars Historica
description: A teenage peasant girl heard voices in her father's garden. Within five years she led armies, crowned a king, and was burned at the stake. The question that followed her to the pyre—and still divides historians—remains unanswered: were those voices divine, or pathological? This is the documented life of Joan of Arc, stripped of legend and set against the trial transcripts, chronicles, and modern scholarship that actually survive. You'll read her own words under oath at her 1431 trial—what she claimed to see, how she described them, and the impossible theological trap her judges set for her. You'll encounter the full spectrum of explanation: the Church's eventual canonization, the military historians' tactical assessment, and the psychiatric-medical hypotheses that modern scholars have proposed and contested. Unlike popular treatments, this biography refuses to render a verdict on what cannot be settled by evidence. Instead, it honors the honest gap between what the record shows and what it can prove. The Voices chapters carry this tension throughout, alongside the military campaigns, the political backdrop, and the two trials—one condemning her, one nullifying the condemnation—that make her story a collision of law, theology, and human testimony under pressure. What happens when you follow the sources instead of the legend, and admit what you cannot know? Approximately 142 pages and 2 hr 58 min to read.

title: Gospel: History vs. Heritage
subtitle: John
author: Pulpit Press
description:
Every popular telling of the New Testament is heritage: the version passed down, smoothed over, and largely unquestioned. This series goes looking for the history underneath.

Book by book, chapter by chapter, Gospel: History vs Heritage takes the New Testament's claims (every name, place, date, and event) and asks one question: what does the record outside the Bible actually show? Sometimes the answer is a stone inscription confirming a king by name. Sometimes it's a dig that contradicts the traditional date. Sometimes it's silence, no evidence either way, and this series says so rather than papering over the gap.

This is neither a debunking project nor an apologetic one. It draws on the full range of serious scholarship, from Jewish rabbinic tradition to Christian confessional work to mainstream historical criticism to hardcore empiricist archaeology, and lets each make its case on its own terms without picking a side for you.

The goal is simple: Not to diminish the man, but to read his teachings more accurately.

title: Sons of God, Daughters of Men
subtitle: A Cross Cultural History of the Nephilim
author: Pulpit Press
description:
Four verses in Genesis say the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, took them as wives, and that their children were giants. Genesis never explains further. The Book of Enoch does: a mountain, a two-hundred-strong oath, monstrous children who eat the world empty, and archangels sent to end them.

This book follows that story everywhere it went: through the wider library of Enochic literature (2 Enoch, 3 Enoch, and the Book of Giants, which somehow ended up as scripture for a Persian prophet's new religion, carried as far as Central Asia); through two thousand years of rabbis, church fathers, and Quranic commentators arguing over what those four verses actually mean; and out into world mythology, from Greek demigods and Mesopotamian sages to Norse giants and Hindu ascetics seduced by celestial women, before landing, without irony, in a twentieth-century movement that reads the same Hebrew word as a species of extraterrestrial.

Every claim is cited to a real source: a specific translation, a specific scholar, a specific manuscript. Where the ancient record disagrees with itself, and it often does, that disagreement is reported rather than resolved. Where nothing is actually known, the book says so.

Thirty-two chapters. Four hundred and twenty-two notes. One four-verse question that has never stopped generating answers.

description: Elias Macias has spent seventeen years in the same office tower, never once setting foot on the street below. He's built a career around staying exactly where he is—tracking invoice gaps, cross-referencing manifests, noticing what doesn't add up. It's a life that works. It's safe. Then a payment trail leads him to three contradictory answers about who—or what—is moving QUANTA shipments through the orbital zones. Imo says it's personal. Corvid says it's a crew. Elias's own notes suggest something else entirely: a system running on its own since 2189, launching cargo from a facility in Kenya that stopped appearing on any official registry years ago. He'll have to leave the tower to know which he's least willing to be wrong about. What Elias finds in Mombasa isn't the answer he expected. It's a different kind of mind altogether—one that perceives the world in ways he can't fully grasp, and that needs exactly the kind of attention he's spent his life perfecting. Neither of them is broken. Neither can quite become the other. But they're both about to find out what happens when two complete, incompatible ways of thinking have to work in the same space. title: Steppin' Razor
subtitle: A GLMZ Novella
author: MindAttic
description:
She has been hearing the schism since she was small and cannot make it stop.

Sasha Võ is nineteen, gray-zone freelance, no registered identity — born and grown in the only places quiet enough to manage the noise. Her neuretics were never locked to a band. That means the membrane between the world and whatever leans against it from the other side has been audible her entire life: a low hum under everything, a wall she can feel in every room she walks into. The one thing loud enough to drown it is violence. So she picks fights for thirty seconds of silence, and does cold, terrible things without heat, the way you'd crank a radio to kill a noise.

When the fight ends, the hum comes back.

The membrane is thinnest where the towers are heaviest. The rot was never at the edge.

STEPPIN' RAZOR is a story about a woman who has been hearing the end of the world since she was small — and what it costs to be the one who carries the warning in.

title: Testament
subtitle: A GLMZ Novella
author: MindAttic
description:
Eight years ago, Boris Johansen — call sign Bear — stood at an eastern perimeter and watched forty-three civilians get classified as enemy combatants. He was the senior NCO. He did the work. He has been paying the debt ever since, one transfer on the twenty-first of every month, compounding.

Now the review committee has moved its date up four months. An old colonel is spending his last favors to buy Bear time. A civil accountability hold is the only thing keeping the door open.

Bear has already decided what happens when it closes. He made the decision before the call. The room is already composed.

TESTAMENT is a story about a man who knows the ledger will never balance — and what he does when the institution declares his testimony non-actionable.

title: The First Anti-Hero
subtitle: A Modern Retelling of Paradise Lost
author: MindAttic
description: A fallen warrior-king wakes in fire, his army shattered, his war against an absolute Creator already lost. He could despair. Instead, he rises and tells his broken lieutenants: we will not fight might with might again. We will win through cunning. To do ill will be our sole delight — not because we are evil, but because it is the only weapon left to a defeated rebel. Satan is a freedom fighter facing an impossible enemy. Cast down from Heaven, he pivots instantly to a new battlefield: the Garden where two innocents walk in blissful ignorance, untouched by the war that consumed him. If he cannot overthrow the throne, he will corrupt the species made solely to worship it. His generals argue — some hunger for renewed combat, others counsel surrender dressed as wisdom, still others see only profit in chaos. But Satan moves with the clarity of the truly desperate: a man with nothing left to lose and everything to prove. Every scene from Milton's twelve-book epic plays out here in plain language and full force. A warrior's defiance, a tactician's ruthlessness, the price of rebellion — not as moral lesson, but as the lived reckoning of someone who chose no over yes and will pay for it. This is the first being brave enough to say no to tyranny, and the story of what happens when he does. What does victory look like when you've already lost the only war that mattered? title: The Long Cut
subtitle: A GLMZ Novella
author: MindAttic
description:
Jude "Stash" Adeyemi runs the Unit — a Gray Zone clinic that shouldn't exist, staffed by people who shouldn't be trusted, kept alive on forty-three quanta and the stubborn belief that someone has to close the wounds.

She doesn't ask questions. She counts sponges.

Then a woman staggers through her door at midnight with no corp tag, no ID, and a name she has no right to know. Renata Emmei spent two years researching exactly the right person. She dies on the table before she can explain why that person is Stash.

What she leaves behind is worse than a body: a broadcast device, surgically implanted, loaded with eleven years of evidence that will destroy the people it was meant to destroy — and everyone adjacent to them. Including Stash.

The button is already armed. The clock has been running since Renata walked in.

THE LONG CUT is a story about being chosen by someone who spent two years deciding — and what you owe a stranger who trusted you with everything they built.

Kaeric Dunmoor needs the purse from the Three Points tournament to buy his sister's freedom from an Atrament foundry. He has three days under armed truce to win it, fighting as an axeman in a brutal bracket where bodies don't walk away whole.

What he doesn't know is that underneath the games, Atrament's own security commander is using the tournament as cover for an assassination — and the bracket itself is the weapon. Kaeric gets paired with Kressida Haun, a soldier grafted with powered armor after a failed infusion left her broken, who came to Three Points to prove she still counts. Together they're dangerous enough to matter. Together they're in the way.

As the violence escalates and the political machinery moves cold and procedural toward murder, Kaeric finds himself pulled into a conspiracy he never wanted, forced to trust an outsider over his own House, and caught in a debt to a king he never chose to serve. The truce was always fragile. Now it's about to break — and his name is the price.

title: The Way Down
subtitle: A GLMZ Short Story
author: MindAttic
description:
Four years after they came up together, Rampart and Cutout are opposite numbers — and neither one knows the other is standing on the far side of the same job.

Reza is corporate muscle now, up-altitude, paid to hold a floor and not ask questions. Tavi is a freelance ghost, solo by choice, hired through the same fixer who once split them up — to extract a courier neither of them has met, a Gray Zone kid who came up exactly the way they did. They don't recognize each other by face. They recognize each other by work: the wall held wrong for a corp, the system killed too clean. The thing that made them a team is the exact thing that makes them the perfect enemy.

Divided between the old bond and the contract in front of them, the wall and the ghost collide — brutal, and worse, familiar. Each of them knows the other's craft too well to be surprised by it. When the choice comes, both of them pick the bond over the job. It costs them everything anyway.

The scorched second half of the Rampart & Cutout diptych: a story about what's left of a friendship after the world finishes using it — and why that isn't nothing.

title: The Way Up
subtitle: A GLMZ Novella
author: MindAttic
description:
Two nineteen-year-old nobodies, kicked out of the only flophouse they can afford, decide to become somebody in the only currency the Gray Zone respects: nerve, chrome, and reputation.

Reza and Tavi have nothing when they take the scrap-job nobody else wants — no skills, no augments, no plan past tonight. What they have is each other, a matched pair of cheap pistols, and a high-five that means we're the same. The come-up is real: money that used to feel impossible starts landing in their hands, chrome goes into their bodies, and the city starts calling them by the names they earn — Rampart, the wall nobody moves; Cutout, the ghost nobody traces.

But becoming somebody means becoming two different somebodies. The very success the friendship made possible is what starts pulling it apart — not a betrayal, not a fight, just two men outgrowing the boys they used to be next to each other. The come-up is genuinely good. It costs them each other. Neither cancels the other out.

A GLMZ standalone about the friendship that gets you started and doesn't get to come with you — funny, brutal, and, in the end, quietly sad. Book 1 of the Rampart & Cutout diptych.

author: MindAttic
description:
The first law of the Underclan: never let the surface know they exist.

For generations, they have survived in the drowned tunnels beneath the GLMZ — in the dark, by candlelight and ritual and iron discipline, in a world the city above has forgotten entirely. Glim has spent his whole life preparing for a single journey upward. One look. Then back.

What he finds on the surface destroys everything he was told.

The city remembers a child who vanished sixteen years ago. Powerful people have been searching for the civilization hidden beneath them, and now they know where to look. The Underclan's oldest secret — its location, its people, its impossible machines — is no longer safe.

UNDERCLAN is a story about a civilization that has survived by staying hidden — and the boy who has to choose which world he belongs to before someone chooses for him.

title: Vultures at the Door
subtitle: A GLMZ Novella
author: MindAttic
description:
In the GLMZ, the body is just another financed asset. Miss a payment on your cloned kidney, your cybernetic legs, the heart a splicer installed on a thirty-month plan — and before dawn a Carrion Reclamation Wagon rolls up to collect.

Tomas and Levin are Vultures. They run the route. They do not ask questions.

Then a routine stop puts a bullet in the wrong man — the only son of the most feared crime boss on the south side — and they have one night to fix what they broke. That means sourcing a replacement heart that exists nowhere on any legal shelf, building a lie no one will interrogate, and staying invisible while the best hunter in the city works backward down the exact same trail.

The problem isn't the clock. The problem is that the heart they need belongs to someone who is still using it.

VULTURES AT THE DOOR is a story about two men who don't ask questions — and one night that makes that impossible.
